관계해석._why_count: A why-question about how many one holder has: why/how come + does X have | X has + that many (+ thing). It asks for the reasons of that holder's current count: the rules and the statements its value rests on.
관계해석._where_owned: Where-questions about a thing someone has: where does X keep the Y, where are X's Y, where is X's Y. The thing is keyed by its owner, as a stated count is.
관계해석._places: A place holds a count like a person: said with its article (the oak cupboard has 18; there are 18 in the oak cupboard; 18 are in the oak cupboard), it receives what is left at, left in or put in it, gives what is taken from it, and both sides of a move (moved, were moved from ... to ...) change. Its name is every word after the article, so a place of several words (the north warehouse) is one holder. Asked: how many are in it, are there in it, does it have.
관계해석._zero_and_only: A zero count is said with the negative determiner no (Haru has no marbles; there are no marbles in the oak cupboard) and is the count 0. 'only has X, N of them' and 'all Haru has is X, N of them' state the count of X after the thing. 'not a single' says the thing in the singular and is the count 0 of its plural (Haru doesn't have a single marble; the oak cupboard doesn't have a single marble). The partitive 'of them' after the count may be left out (Haru only has marbles, 18).
관계해석._vague: A count not given yet: 'some' before the thing (Haru has some marbles; the oak cupboard has some marbles; there are some marbles in it; Haru has 18 marbles and some pears) is recorded as a count not known (count_unknown), and a question about it is held. The number said later without its holder (18 of them; there are 18 of them; it's 18 marbles; Haru has 18 of them) is the count of the one count not known yet that it fits: the last one said, the one of that thing, or the one of that holder.
관계해석._use_for: Things used for a purpose leave the holder; the purpose after 'for the' fills no holder (Haru used 2 marbles for the party).
관계해석._two_of_them: 'the two of them' and 'both of them' ask the sum of exactly two holders of the thing; with more holders the question does not say which two and is not answered.

문장분리._설명: Clause boundaries are punctuation and declared connectives. A comma splits only when the part before it is a complete clause.
문장분리._time_order: Order in time: a question about the state just before or just after one earlier event, joined to the event by the subordinating conjunction before or after, on either side (How many figs did Ada have before Ada gave Bo 2? / After Ada gave Bo 2, how many figs did Bo have?). The event side names the holders who took part and may name the amount; exactly one earlier event must fit.
문장분리._relative_clauses: The non-restrictive relative clause: a relative pronoun (who for people, which for things -- the two of English; that and whom do not open one between commas) after its one-word head and a comma, closed by the next comma (Moru, who has 2 marbles, gave Haru 1). When it states an amount it is said as its own clause first, with the head as its subject (Moru has 2 marbles. Moru gave Haru 1).

활용._설명: Only declared verbs inflect. Irregular forms are listed in the lexicon; a verb not listed takes the declared regular suffix. Nothing is guessed from an input word.

_자리조사: English marks roles by position and prepositions, not particles.
_부정: English negates a clause with do-support: a form of do, the particle not (or the contraction n't) and the bare verb (Haru did not give Moru 2 marbles; Haru doesn't have 18 marbles; they don't own any). The form of do carries the verb's tense and person: did -> the past, does -> the third person present, do -> the base. A negated clause is read as its positive clause, not asserted: a transfer that did not happen moves nothing, a count denied is not the count. The verb must be one this pack inflects (its lexicon or a same-frame stem).
_지시어: Words that point back at something already said in this conversation. When several things fit, ask; never pick.
_사람지시어: The pointers of 지시어 that point back at a person, the closed class in full: a place this conversation holds things in is never what they mean.

군말._설명: Sentence-initial words that carry no content. The original text still competes; a reading without them is only an extra candidate.

문서분류._설명: Surface shapes of English document sentences.

_이음어미: English joins clauses with words, not endings; this never matches.

생략._설명: coordination: a conjunct after a comma that leaves out the trailing words of the previous conjunct's subject inherits them (Minsu has five apples, and Jiyeon has two -> Jiyeon apples). part_reference: naming only the leading word of a known subject names that subject when exactly one fits. scope 'turn': the coordination ellipsis holds between any two clauses of one turn, whatever joins them -- a comma, a connective, or the period between two sentences said together (Minsu has five apples. Jiyeon has two). gapping 'first_conjunct_verb': a later conjunct of a count statement may leave out the verb it shares with the clause before, and with it the holder or the thing counted (Minsu has five apples and Jiyeon two; Minsu has five apples and two pears): it is read as that clause with the conjunct's words in their places. counted_noun 'after_numeral': a count statement whose example says so (counted_noun: may_elide) may leave out the counted noun after its numeral when the conversation has named it (gave 2 to Bo, left 3 at the shed; what 'gave 2 of them to Bo' reads as); each holder is then named alone and found by its leading words, as part_reference says.

수선._설명: Edits that bring an unmatched clause to the nearest declared rule. Only typed words move, drop or swap; nothing untyped and undeclared is added. Over the bound the clause is held and the needed edit is named.
수선._protected: Words a repair may never change: it may not skip, swap, move a particle onto or off, or put into a name any numeral (the declared numerals and digits), counter (수량단위, none in English), scope word or negation. Scope words: the English quantifiers and totalisers that decide which holders an amount covers (both, together, altogether, all, each, every, total, combined, apiece, either, neither, sum). Negation: the negative particle not/n't and the negative determiners and pronouns (no, never, none, nothing, nobody, neither, nor, without). A turn whose nearest repair would change one of them is held, and the reply names the word. A negation (negation_in_names: all of them in English) is also refused inside a name that a declared rule read directly ('Ada figs not').

_명사수: An item counted as one is written in the singular (one marble, 1 box) but names the same things as its plural (marbles). A fact about exactly one is keyed by the plural computed here, so 'Haru had one marble' and 'how many marbles does Haru have' meet. Only the last word of the item changes; the first matching row wins, and a word already ending in the plural s stays as it is. In a partitive or measure phrase (a jar of jam, a box of crayons) the number is marked on the measure noun before 'of' (jars of jam), so that word takes the plural. The irregular plurals are looked up before the rows, whole word only (a word like 'human' is not 'man'): the closed classes of English irregular plural nouns -- vowel mutation (man, woman, foot, tooth, goose, mouse, louse), the -en plurals (child, ox), the suppletive person/people, the zero plurals (sheep, deer, fish, moose, swine, bison, salmon, trout, cod, aircraft, series, species, offspring), the f/fe nouns that voice to -ves (knife, wife, life, leaf, loaf, wolf, calf, half, shelf, thief, scarf, elf, self, sheaf) and the consonant + o nouns that take -oes (potato, tomato, hero, echo, veto, torpedo).
_같은틀: Verbs that take the frame of a verb the examples already use. Every form the inflection grammar computes for these stems (hands, handed, lent, owns, used ...) is also read as the word the examples are written with. The frame's roles and meaning are the example's; only the verb word changes. A verb not listed here is not read. Rows are whole verb classes: 'gave' — Levin (1993) §13.1 give verbs (feed, give, lease, lend, loan, pass, pay, peddle, refund, render, rent, repay, sell, serve, trade) and §11.1 send verbs (hand, send, mail, post, ship, deliver, forward, return, transfer, dispatch, convey, transport, slip, smuggle, sneak, shunt, port; the brand-name verbs airmail, express, FedEx, UPS are not entered); 'have' (row with 'as': each form read as the same form of have: owns -> has, own -> have, owned -> had) — stative verbs of possession (own, possess, hold, keep, carry); 'lost' — verbs of consumption and loss, the thing leaves the holder (eat, drink, use, spend, consume, waste, lose); 'got' — verbs of obtaining (Levin §13.5.2 obtain verbs: borrow, buy, purchase, obtain, acquire, collect, accept, win, earn, inherit, and find): with a 'from' source the source loses what the subject gains ('Haru got 2 marbles from Moru'), without one the subject gains ('Haru got 2 marbles').
_말바꿈: Phrases read as another phrase, one more candidate beside the typed text: a contraction of have got; a partitive 'of them/hers' that leaves the item to the elided frame ('gave Moru 2'); a time word that places the event but changes no role, and the adverbs of repetition (again, once again, once more; the class the Korean pack declares as 또, 다시); a title before a name. A phrase not listed is not rewritten. The progressive of the stative possession verbs that take it (be + holding/keeping/carrying) reads as has (is) or had (was); a plural subject is read by no count statement of this pack. Time and aspect adverbs that place a state but change no role are left out (now, still, currently, right now, at the moment, at present, so far, by now), wherever they stand. Partitives with a determiner leave the determiner phrase to the noun (two of her/his/their/my/your/our/its/the/these/those figs = two figs). Phrasal particles of transfer and consumption verbs are read with the verb (handed over, passed on, gave back, handed back, paid back = gave/handed/passed/paid; gave away = lost, the receiver unnamed; used up, ate up, drank up = used/ate/drank). Expressions of the initial state are left out (at first, at the start, at the beginning, in the beginning, to begin with, initially, originally) and 'started (out) with', 'began with' read as had. Additive quantifiers after a numeral add nothing to the amount (2 more, extra, additional, further figs = 2 figs). The degree phrases of a why-question about an amount read alike (so many, so few, that few, this many, this few = that many). Being responsible for a count is having it (is/was responsible for = has/had). The discourse adverbs that place or source a statement but change no role are left out (after that, afterwards, apparently; too, also; by the way, to be exact, I just counted, not sure how many), and 'at all' after a zero. 'the same' before the counted noun names the kind already said and adds nothing (the same 4 pillows = 4 pillows). The negated possessive with 'any' or 'a single' is a zero count: doesn't have any / hasn't got any / doesn't have a single = has no (don't, haven't: have no). The indefinite article before a counted noun is the numeral one (got a fig = got 1 fig). The article is the numeral one only before a counted noun: the vague quantity idioms (a lot of, lots of, a few, a couple of, a bunch of, a handful of, a number of, a little, a bit of) say 'some', a count not known, and 'a total of' before a numeral adds nothing.

_이름답: A reply that only names a person. After a question held for its pointer, the name answers which one; otherwise it asks the last answered question about that person. These words may stand before the name; anything else means it is not such a reply. Heads are the discourse connectives that open a follow-up (and, so, then, but, also), the elliptical question openers (what about, how about, what of) and the reformulations (I mean, I meant); several may stand one after another (and how about ...). A head may be followed by a comma (Sorry, I meant Haru). Tails are the reformulations said after the name (Haru, I mean; Haru is who I meant; Haru is the one I meant), and the apologies and interjections that open a self-repair (sorry, oh, no, wait, actually) are heads. The name may carry a title or a relation; it is read as the pack reads a holder.
_대조정정: A correction said as a contrast of two amounts: 'Actually it was one, not two.' The amount before the marker is the new one, the one after it the old one. The one earlier statement that carried the old amount is corrected in place; no new event is added. Several such statements are asked back. restate_heads: a correction said by restating the event with its new amount after a head that says the earlier statement was wrong (Sorry, I misspoke: Haru gave Moru 1). The heads are phrases that say one's own statement was wrong, and the editing term 'I mean(t)' of self-repair (Levelt 1983); the event is named by any form of a verb of its frame.
_수동태: The be-passive of a transfer verb with its recipient and agent: 'N things were given to B by A' is read as 'A gave B N things'. The auxiliary is any finite form of be that agrees with a singular or plural theme (is, are, was, were); the participle must be the declared participle of a verb this pack reads. Without both 'to' and 'by' nothing is read: the giver or the receiver would be guessed.
_요청: Request mood. An utterance that opens with a request word or a modal request (please, kindly, let's, let us, can/could/would/will you) or closes with 'please' or 'for me' asks for an action; it reports no event, so if nothing reads it, it is not kept as an unread event that holds later questions.
_이름밖: Words that are never part of a holder's or a thing's name in a reading: the English prepositions (all of them but 'of', which a partitive keeps: boxes of crayons; with 'than', so 'Ada has 2 more figs than Bo' is not read as a count of 'figs than Bo') and the adverbial particles away, back. A name that holds one swallowed a phrase the example does not have ('figs to Bo', 'figs at first'), so that reading is not taken.
_가진쪽꼴: How a holder is said when it is not a bare name, each form read as the one name the facts use. self: the English first-person pronoun in every case (I; me, myself) reads as I, the pack's 임자자리말; its contractions (I've, I'm, I'd) are said in full; a verb after it agrees as after any other holder, the examples being written in the third person (the verbs whose present differs by person: be, have, do, and the stative possession verbs own, hold, keep, carry), and in a question the auxiliary before it agrees the same way (do I have -> does I have). possessives + a relation noun + a name (close apposition: my cousin Ana, our aunt Ana, Lind's cousin Ana): the name is the holder (the possessive determiners of English, all of them, and the possessive 's). determiners: a determiner, a role of one to three words, a comma, a name and a comma (the courier, Lind, ...): the name is the holder. self_possessives: the user's own relation with no name after it (my sister) is the relation noun. numeral_articles: 'the' before a numeral (gave back the two figs) adds nothing to the amount, unless a partitive follows (the two of them). A name is a capitalised word. prefix_titles: the English courtesy titles before a surname (Mr., Ms., Mrs., Dr., written with or without the period) name the holder by the surname. leading_modifiers: the adverbial particles that are outside names (back, away) may still open a place's name as its modifier (the back hall), never follow a name (figs back).
_말자리: Phrases said away from where the examples have them. A fronted recipient: the preposition to and a name before a comma open the clause (To Bo, Ada gave 2 figs) and are read at its end (Ada gave 2 figs to Bo). A fronted purpose: the preposition for and a phrase before a comma open the clause (For the trip, Ada lent Bo 2 figs) and are left out; a purpose fills no role. A shifted particle: the particle of a phrasal transfer verb (back, over: gave back, handed over) said after a one-word object (gave Bo back 2) is read after the verb.
